title: Kth Number in Dictionary Order
statement:
Write the numbers 1 to n as text and sort them the way a dictionary would, character by character. For n = 12 the order is 1, 10, 11, 12, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, the same order a file browser uses for names like 10.png and 2.png when it has no "natural sort".

Return the k-th number in that order, counting from 1. n can be up to a billion, so listing the numbers is too slow.

examples.why: 1, 10, 100: a number comes right after its own prefix.
1 and 10–19 make the first 11 entries; 20 comes only after 2.

hints: Picture all the numbers as a tree of digits: 1 has children 10–19, 10 has children 100–109, and so on. Dictionary order is a preorder walk of that tree.
Walking node by node costs k steps. Can you skip a whole subtree at once if you know how many numbers ≤ n it holds?

Count the subtree under prefix p level by level: the range [p, p] on the first level, [10p, 10p + 9] on the next, each clipped at n. If the count is at most the remaining k, skip to p + 1; otherwise step down to 10p.

explain.intuition:
The numbers form a ten-way tree of prefixes: below 1 sit 10 … 19, below 10 sit 100 … 109. Reading the tree in preorder gives dictionary order. So you are asked for the k-th node of a preorder walk, and the trick is to skip subtrees you know you will not enter.

The size of the subtree under prefix p is easy to count: on each level its numbers form one contiguous range, [p, p], then [10p, 10p + 9], then [100p, 100p + 99], each clipped to n. That takes about 10 levels. If the whole subtree fits in the steps still left, jump over it to the sibling p + 1. If not, the answer is inside it: step down to the first child 10p, which costs one step.
steps: Start at cur = 1 with k − 1 steps left, since 1 itself is the first entry.
While steps remain, count the numbers in the subtree under cur: sum min(n, last) − first + 1 over levels, with first = cur, last = cur and then first ×= 10, last = last × 10 + 9, while first ≤ n.
If that count is ≤ the steps left, subtract it and move to cur + 1.
pitfalls: Generating the numbers as strings and sorting them. With n up to 10⁹ that is far too much memory and time.
Clipping the level range with n + 1 instead of n, or letting last stay unclipped. Both overcount the subtree near the top end.
Forgetting that stepping down to 10p uses one step, because you pass over p itself.

solutions.title: Walk the order one step at a time
solutions.idea: Generate dictionary order with a next-number rule: go to 10·cur if allowed, otherwise climb up past trailing 9s and n, then add 1.

solutions.title: Skip whole prefix subtrees
solutions.idea: Count how many numbers ≤ n start with the current prefix; skip the prefix if they all come before the answer, otherwise descend.

followups: Return all numbers from 1 to n in dictionary order using O(1) extra space. (That is the step-by-step walk above.)
Given a number x ≤ n, return its position in dictionary order.
